Key Innovation: Settling a file transfer on cryptographic proof of content: the hold invoice releases only when the requester's SHA-256 of the downloaded data matches the torrent's expected hash, so the escrow is resolved by the data itself rather than by either party's claim, with collateral bonds on both sides removing the incentive to grief.
Core Problem: Data on peer-to-peer networks dies quietly. A torrent with zero seeders is functionally lost even though copies still sit on hard drives, because reseeding costs bandwidth and time and returns nothing to the person who does it. The existing workarounds — private trackers, invite-gated forums, reseed request threads — are social favours that do not scale and mostly fail.
Solution: Turn reseeding into a paid bounty settled trustlessly. The requester locks a Bitcoin reward in a Lightning hold invoice and posts the missing pieces; a hunter joins and both sides post collateral bonds; the hunter seeds over WebTorrent; the requester hashes what arrives and the backend settles only on a SHA-256 match, returning funds automatically otherwise. Authentication is a wallet signature, so there are no accounts to create.
Target Users: Archivists, researchers and users trying to recover unavailable files, and holders of rare data willing to reseed for payment.
Unique Insight: Torrent decay is an incentive problem, not a technical one, and Lightning micropayments are finally small and fast enough to price a single act of reseeding.
Differentiation: Differs from private trackers, which use ratio economics and social gatekeeping, by paying in real money and requiring no membership, and from paid file hosting by keeping distribution peer-to-peer.
Reusable Patterns: Hash-verified escrow settlement, two-sided collateral bonds against griefing, hold-invoice HTLCs for conditional Lightning payment, and wallet-signature authentication are reusable across any deliver-and-verify marketplace.
Business Model: Inference: not stated. A percentage of each bounty or a flat routing fee on settlement is the natural revenue line, though the design would work equally as a public good.
Moat: Inference: not stated. The compounding asset would be the index of revived torrents and the roster of hunters holding rare data.
Distribution Strategy: Inference: not stated. Data-hoarding and archival communities are dense and self-organising, which makes them an efficient first channel.
Key Risks: Paying for the redistribution of arbitrary torrents carries obvious copyright exposure that the design does not address; and the system settles on hash match, which proves delivery but not that the requester is entitled to the content.
New Idea Opportunities: Inference: the same bounty-plus-hash-escrow mechanism is a general primitive for paid data availability — reviving research datasets, IPFS pins or archived web content — where the legal position is far cleaner than for torrents.

Summary: Tabula is a zero-knowledge kernel for tabular state transitions. It moves the proving abstraction from ISA-level execution to schema-typed state transitions, so memory-consistency cost scales with the number of state accesses rather than with total computation.
Problem Solved: General-purpose zkVMs such as SP1 and RISC Zero prove machine execution, which is structurally wasteful for stateful applications: every state access goes through the full ISA pipeline, the sorted-memory argument must cover stack frames and heap allocations as well as application state, memory is untyped so no type-aware optimisation is possible, and state-root computation is pushed to the application, where updating 100 accounts in a depth-20 Merkle tree costs on the order of 2,000 hashes all proven as ISA execution.
How It Works: Tabula distinguishes stateful computation (persistent reads and writes, expensive because of ISA overhead, memory consistency and state-root hashing) from stateless computation (arithmetic, comparisons, hashing — localised, fixed constraints per operation). Rather than equalising their marginal cost through a shared ISA trace, it makes schema-typed tables the primitive, so the prover knows a column holds u64 values or that a table has 50 rows and can exploit that. The public artefact takes sealed program semantics plus typed table state, executes a stateful transaction batch, and verifies the resulting proof against an explicit expected public statement.
Project Chain or Network: Chain-agnostic zero-knowledge proving infrastructure; targets rollup state-transition proving
Tech Stack: Rust; STARK proving; schema-typed tabular state model; statement-first verification against a published public_statement.json. Repository topics: rust, stark, zkp.

Key Innovation: Moving the proving abstraction boundary from the instruction set to schema-typed state transitions, so that memory consistency is argued only over actual state accesses rather than over stack, heap and temporaries, and the prover can exploit type information that an untyped byte-array memory model discards.
Core Problem: General-purpose zkVMs charge the same marginal proving cost for an arithmetic comparison and a database read, because both become RISC-V instructions in one trace. For a batch of 100 balance transfers the business logic is trivial — read, compare, subtract, add, write — yet almost all the constraints go to ISA overhead, memory consistency over stack and heap, and roughly 2,000 hashes for the Merkle state root, so the actual application semantics are a small fraction of the proof.
Solution: Make schema-typed tables the proving primitive instead of a flat byte array. Separate stateful from stateless computation so each is charged its true cost, constrain memory consistency only over real state accesses, let the prover exploit column types and table sizes, and manage state commitment inside the kernel rather than pushing Merkle hashing into application-level ISA instructions.

Core Problem: Every privacy wallet still has to ask a centralised RPC provider to verify state, and that request leaks the user's IP address, the addresses being queried, request timing and behavioural patterns, on top of the email and card details used to buy the plan. Solution: A two-part stack: a Tor hidden-service RPC gateway that validates an x402 USDC micropayment per request and proxies to an execution node without logging, and an Electron wallet that embeds Helios WASM so non-state calls never leave the device while an Arti Tor toggle anonymises the remaining eth_getProof traffic. Target Users: Privacy-focused wallet users and the wallet developers building the fat privacy stacks that currently stop at the RPC boundary.
Unique Insight: Privacy engineering has focused on what the transaction reveals while ignoring that the act of reading the chain reveals just as much — and that the subscription payment for reading is itself the strongest identifier.
Differentiation: Differs from Infura and Alchemy by collecting no metadata and requiring no account, from raw Tor by having a sustainable per-request payment model, and from Nym by shipping production-ready Arti with an integrated wallet.
Reusable Patterns: Pay-per-request infrastructure over x402, Tor hidden services as a privacy layer for API access, and vendored WASM light clients for local verification are reusable across privacy infrastructure.

Summary: BORDEL-gate is an on- and off-chain authentication protocol that turns NFC wristbands and wallets into cryptographic access credentials for a community space, using zero-knowledge membership proofs so a member can open a door without revealing which member they are or exposing the membership list.
Problem Solved: The BORDEL community currently manages access with Merkle-tree memberships and multiple verification mechanisms, but memberships stay publicly visible on-chain, permissions are hard to change dynamically, and access control depends on fragmented, partly centralised infrastructure.
How It Works: A member enrols an ECDSA secp256k1 public key — from a HaLo NFC chip or an EOA wallet — as a Poseidon leaf in a Merkle tree, which updates the root. To gain access the member signs a fresh EIP-712 challenge with the same key and generates a Noir zero-knowledge proof that both the signature is valid and the signing key's leaf is in the tree, without revealing the key or which member they are. The protocol checks that the member is valid, currently holds that capability, and that the proof is fresh and non-replayable, then the resolver returns the wallet address and access is granted. The whole app is client-side with the membership tree in browser localStorage and no backend or database.

Summary: SignGuard is a browser-extension transaction-understanding layer that pauses a MetaMask request before final confirmation and explains what the transaction actually does — using simulation, calldata decoding, contract inspection, approval analysis, ENS verification, Sourcify source verification, phishing detection and protocol identification — rather than reducing it to a green or red safety label.

Existing security tools answer only whether something is safe or unsafe, which does not tell the user what permissions are being granted, which assets can move, who they are interacting with, or whether it matches their intent. Summary: Lumen is a cryptographically safe whistleblowing protocol. A worker proves they are a verified employee of a company without revealing who they are, using a RISC Zero ZK-STARK anchored to a Poseidon Merkle tree of employee badges managed on-chain; the report goes to IPFS and the proof to Sepolia, so no party — company, platform or Lumen itself — can link a submission to an individual.

Summary: Penumbra brings sealed-bid auctions to Ethereum using zero-knowledge proofs. Bid amounts and bidder identities never appear on-chain — not even after the auction closes — and the winner claims tokens by proving knowledge of a secret rather than by revealing who they are.
Problem Solved: On a public blockchain every bid is visible in real time, which causes three failures: later bidders see existing bids and outbid by the minimum, suppressing the true price; bidder addresses are public and link financial activity to real identities; and bots front-run visible bid data before finalisation. The winner proves knowledge of the secret with a ZK proof generated server-side and submitted from a burner wallet, so the winner's real address never touches the claim transaction. A nullifier scheme prevents either side from cheating. Stealth address spending and viewing keypairs are derived deterministically from wallet signatures without private keys ever reaching a server, and BitGo custody handles private ETH deposits per bidder.

Summary: MeshSearch is private web search for humans and AI agents. Queries are ZK-committed client-side before leaving the device, paid per search with USDC over x402, routed through three ENS-named relay hops, and stored as AES-256-GCM encrypted history on Fileverse under the user's wallet key. Target Users: Privacy-conscious users, and developers building AI agents that search the web on a user's behalf.
Unique Insight: Agent traffic is where private search matters most and where it is easiest to adopt, because an agent's search tool is a configuration line rather than a browser habit users must change.
Differentiation: Differs from privacy search engines by removing the need to trust the operator at all, and from Tor-based approaches by making relay operators nameable through ENS and payable through unlinkable addresses.
Reusable Patterns: ENS-named auditable relay routing, ZK query commitments, x402 anonymous per-use payment, and stealth-address operator payouts are reusable across privacy infrastructure.
Business Model: Stated in the design: per-search x402 USDC micropayments, with relay operators paid from that flow. Inference: the protocol's own margin is not published.
Moat: Inference: not stated. Relay-operator coverage and the auditable reputation of those operators would be the compounding asset.
Distribution Strategy: Inference: not stated. Shipping as an MCP server means distribution runs through agent tool registries and developer configs rather than consumer marketing.
Key Risks: Three-hop routing plus ZK commitment adds latency that agents may not tolerate; the exit relay still sees the decrypted query against the upstream engine; and relay operator collusion breaks the anonymity set.
New Idea Opportunities: Inference: the ENS-named relay pattern could become a general standard for auditable mixnets, and the same MCP-plus-x402 shape applies to any private data tool an agent needs.

Summary: Mosaik is a covenant DEX on the Liquid Network with no order book, no matching engine and no maker server. Every order is a Tessera — a single Liquid UTXO governed by a Simplicity covenant that enforces its own trade terms — and a market is simply a mosaic of those coins.
Problem Solved: On every exchange, centralised or not, an order is a promise: the venue holds the funds, the market maker can renege, and each hop between trader and trade is another party to trust. Even non-custodial DEXs rely on a matching engine or a maker who must stay online.
How It Works: A maker locks asset A into one Liquid UTXO controlled by a Tessera covenant. The covenant uses Simplicity's transaction introspection to read the transaction trying to spend it, and offers two doors. SETTLE is spendable by anyone but only by a transaction that pays the maker exactly the asked amount of asset B, so a taker physically cannot take asset A without paying. REFUND is keyless: after a timeout anyone can sweep the coin, but only back to the maker, so the maker can stay offline indefinitely without stranding funds. Offers are discovered over a Nostr orderbook and a browser wallet lets both sides fund, make and fill.

Summary: Cocoa Monster is a privacy-first prediction market on Midnight where market prices and resolutions stay publicly verifiable while individual positions, amounts and identities remain private through zero-knowledge proofs. It supports YES/NO markets and multi-option markets with up to eight options under one question.
Problem Solved: Prediction markets are valuable because they turn collective belief into a price, but most on-chain markets also turn every trader's behaviour into public metadata: addresses, balances, timing and portfolio history. The question the team set was whether the public price and verifiable settlement can be kept while removing the public per-user position book.
How It Works: Each market is a constant-product market maker where reserveYes multiplied by reserveNo stays constant; buying YES burns YES reserve and grows NO reserve in proportion to the stake, so price floats and a live chart can be derived from on-chain reserve deltas. Positions are committed on-chain as a hash of secret, nonce, side and amount, which hides identity, side and size. Markets close on-chain and redemption reveals only a one-shot nullifier, so a winner can claim without linking their claim to their original position.

Summary: Veil Protocol is a privacy-native payment layer for autonomous agents. A sender derives a fresh one-time stealth address for each payment from the receiver's public keys, so no observer can link sender to receiver, and the receiver scans encrypted announcements to find payments addressed to them.

Key Innovation: Committing both sides of the game before it starts: the player's card and the caller's number sequence are each fixed by a commitment, so neither a player claiming a card they did not hold nor a caller reordering draws to favour someone can succeed, while the card itself stays private during play.

Differentiation: Differs from online bingo platforms by making the operator unable to alter the draw, and from provably-fair casino RNG schemes by also committing the player's card so claims cannot be fabricated.
Reusable Patterns: Pre-commitment of both operator randomness and participant state, claim verification against multiple independent conditions, and public audit trails for dispute resolution are reusable across raffles, lotteries and giveaways.

New Idea Opportunities: Inference: the commit-both-sides pattern is directly applicable to raffles and charity draws, and packaging it as a verifiable-draw service for existing operators would avoid the consumer adoption problem entirely.

Summary: Dojo is a training ground for AI agents on BNB Chain. Summary: FairDrop is a zero-knowledge identity and access protocol that enforces one-human-one-action on HashKey Chain. Users prove membership in an identity set with Groth16 proofs without revealing personal data, enabling fair airdrops, private voting and compliant token access.
Problem Solved: Airdrop farming, multi-wallet voting manipulation, private-sale abuse and weak access control all stem from the same gap: systems can verify that an address acted but not that a distinct human is behind it, so anyone with many wallets captures a disproportionate share.
How It Works: The core inversion is that FairDrop does not verify who a user is but that this is a valid unique identity and it has not acted before. Identity is generated locally as a nullifier and trapdoor pair, a Poseidon commitment is stored on-chain, and membership is tracked in a Merkle tree registry. Each action type uses a domain-separated nullifier — FAIRDROP_AIRDROP_V1, FAIRDROP_VOTE_V1, FAIRDROP_ACCESS_V1, FAIRDROP_PRIVATE_SALE_V1 — so an identity can claim once per domain without linking its actions across domains. Progressive staking raises the cost of each additional join, adding an economic sybil deterrent on top of the cryptographic one.
Tech Stack: Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs; Poseidon hash commitments; Merkle tree membership registry; domain-separated nullifiers; progressive staking for sybil resistance; deployed at zk-fairdrop.vercel.app.

Key Innovation: Domain-separated nullifiers: an identity gets exactly one action per domain — one airdrop claim, one vote, one sale participation — while the nullifiers for different domains cannot be linked to each other, so uniqueness is enforced per context without building a cross-context profile of the user.
Core Problem: Every open distribution mechanism in crypto is captured by whoever can afford the most wallets. Airdrops are farmed at industrial scale, votes are bought by splitting holdings, private sales are gamed by the same buyers under multiple identities, and access control degrades to address allowlists that anyone can multiply. Verifying identity would fix it but requires collecting exactly the personal data users and regulators both object to.
Solution: Prove uniqueness instead of identity. Generate an identity locally as a nullifier and trapdoor, commit it on-chain with Poseidon, track membership in a Merkle tree, and let a Groth16 proof demonstrate set membership without revealing anything. Domain-separated nullifiers cap each identity to one action per context, and progressive staking makes each additional registration more expensive than the last.
Target Users: Protocols running airdrops, DAOs running votes, and issuers running private sales or gated access on HashKey Chain.
Unique Insight: Sybil resistance does not require knowing who someone is, only proving that this identity has not already acted in this context — which is a strictly weaker and therefore achievable requirement.
Differentiation: Differs from KYC gating by revealing no personal data, and from proof-of-personhood networks by working from a project-controlled identity set rather than requiring global enrolment.
Reusable Patterns: Domain-separated nullifiers for per-context uniqueness, Poseidon commitments in Merkle membership registries, and progressive staking as an economic sybil deterrent are reusable across identity and distribution systems.

Distribution Strategy: Inference: not stated. Being adopted as the default sybil gate for HashKey ecosystem airdrops would populate the identity set fastest.
Key Risks: The security of the whole system rests on how identities enter the Merkle set, which is not described — if registration is open, sybil resistance reduces to the progressive staking cost; and the private repository prevents any review of the circuits.

Summary: ZKGate lets users prove KYC compliance, age and jurisdiction on HashKey Chain with Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs, disclosing no personal data. It supports selective disclosure of individual attributes, ZK-gated DeFi access and private airdrops.
Problem Solved: Every DeFi protocol faces a binary choice: require KYC and permanently expose user identity on-chain, or stay anonymous and be excluded from regulated markets. There is no mechanism that satisfies a regulator's requirement and a user's privacy at the same time.
How It Works: Three stages. Issue: the user submits KYC data, a Poseidon hash commitment is generated and added to an on-chain Merkle tree, and the raw data never touches the blockchain. Verify: the proof is submitted to the ZKGate contract, which confirms the claimed attributes without learning anything else.

Summary: HSK Passport is a shared compliance layer for HashKey Chain: a user verifies once with a regulated KYC provider and receives a Semaphore zero-knowledge credential, after which any regulated dApp can gate access with a single require line while leaving zero personally identifiable information on-chain.
Problem Solved: Every regulated dApp on a chain rebuilds its own KYC integration, and each one collects and stores the same identity data again. On-chain, verification either exposes the user's identity or links all their activity across applications, which is unacceptable to users and increasingly to regulators.
How It Works: A user verifies once through Sumsub — the same regulated KYC provider HashKey Exchange uses — and receives a Semaphore zero-knowledge credential bound to their wallet. Any HashKey Chain dApp then calls passport.verifyCredential(groupId, proof), or in v6 HSKPassportFreshness.verifyFresh(...) to additionally require the credential was issued within a freshness window the dApp chooses. The worked example in the project's own vision is precise about what is and is not revealed: a contract selling tokenised silver learns the buyer is KYC verified and that the credential is fresh, but not her name, passport number, verification date, or that she is the same person who bought a different token yesterday.
Tech Stack: TypeScript and Solidity with Circom circuits; Semaphore zero-knowledge credentials; Sumsub as the regulated KYC issuer; HSKPassportFreshness contract for credential freshness windows; a Policy Composer tool; deployed at hskpassport.gudman.xyz. MIT licensed.

Key Innovation: Adding a dApp-chosen freshness window to a zero-knowledge KYC credential: verifyFresh lets each application require that the credential was issued recently without learning when, which is the property that makes a one-time verification acceptable to regulators who care that compliance is current rather than historical.
Core Problem: Regulated applications on a public chain face a compliance dilemma with no good answer. Requiring KYC per application means every dApp separately collects and stores identity data, multiplying breach surface and cost, and any on-chain record of verification either exposes the user or links their entire activity across applications. Staying anonymous means being excluded from regulated markets entirely.
Solution: Verify once with Sumsub, the regulated issuer the ecosystem's exchange already uses, and receive a Semaphore credential bound to the wallet. Every dApp then gates with a single require line calling verifyCredential or verifyFresh, sharing one privacy-preserving credential pool. The contract learns only that the user is verified and that the credential is fresh — no name, no document number, no verification date, and no linkage across applications.
Target Users: Regulated dApps on HashKey Chain such as tokenised RWA issuers, and their users who must satisfy KYC without publishing identity.
Unique Insight: Compliance and privacy conflict only because verification is re-performed and re-recorded per application; verify once into a shared credential pool and both requirements are satisfiable simultaneously.
Differentiation: Differs from per-dApp KYC by sharing one credential pool across the ecosystem, and from generic ZK identity by anchoring to the regulated issuer the ecosystem's own exchange already relies on.

Summary: Jing Swap is a blind batch auction for sBTC/STX and sBTC/USDCx that settles at the Pyth oracle spot price rather than along an AMM curve, so a trade of any size clears at the same rate with no slippage, front-running or sandwich risk. The team reports $60K cleared in mainnet beta.
Problem Solved: Large sBTC/STX swaps on AMM DEXs get worse prices the bigger they are: slippage scales with size, MEV bots sandwich the transaction, and the trade moves the market against itself. Treasuries, stacking pools and miners therefore trade off-chain, taking custody risk on pool yield, routing through centralised exchanges and paying 1–2% in fees and spreads — so the Stacks ecosystem could not use its own infrastructure for large swaps.
How It Works: Depositors lock sBTC, STX or USDCx into a pool while the settlement price is unknown, which makes front-running mathematically impossible because there is no price to trade ahead of. Deposits stay open for a minimum of 150 blocks (about five minutes) until someone calls close-deposits, then a 30-block buffer (~60 seconds) elapses before settlement clears at the Pyth oracle spot price. Three safety gates validate the oracle: staleness under 60 seconds, confidence interval under 2%, and a DEX sanity check within 10% of BitFlow. Everyone in the batch receives the same rate, tokens are pushed directly to wallets with no claim step, and unfilled amounts automatically roll into the next batch.
Project Chain or Network: Stacks (Bitcoin L2); sBTC, STX and USDCx
Tech Stack: Clarity smart contracts implementing the blind batch auction; Pyth oracle price feeds with staleness, confidence and cross-DEX sanity gates; BitFlow as the sanity reference; JavaScript tooling.

Key Innovation: Making front-running impossible by construction rather than by mitigation: depositors commit before any settlement price exists, and a 30-block buffer plus oracle-clearing means the price is determined after commitment — so there is nothing to sandwich, nothing to reorder and no size-dependent slippage, with everyone in the batch receiving the identical rate.
Core Problem: Automated market makers price a trade as a function of its size, so the participants who most need to move sBTC — treasuries, stacking pools and miners — get the worst execution and are also the most attractive MEV targets. The rational response is to leave the chain entirely: route through a centralised exchange, accept custody risk on pooled yield, and pay 1–2% in fees and spread. That leaves the ecosystem unable to use its own DeFi for meaningful size.
Solution: Run a blind batch auction. Depositors lock sBTC, STX or USDCx for at least 150 blocks with no visible settlement price; after close-deposits and a 30-block buffer the batch clears at the Pyth oracle spot price, validated by staleness, confidence and cross-DEX sanity gates. Every participant gets the same rate regardless of size, tokens push straight to wallets, and unfilled amounts roll forward automatically.
Target Users: Stacks treasuries, stacking pools, miners and any trader moving size in sBTC.
Unique Insight: Competing with AMMs on speed is hopeless, but AMMs are structurally incapable of giving a large order a fair price — so a venue that trades latency for price integrity wins exactly the flow AMMs serve worst.
Differentiation: Differs from AMM DEXs by settling at oracle spot rather than along a curve, and from centralised exchange OTC desks by remaining fully on-chain and non-custodial.
Reusable Patterns: Blind commitment before price discovery, batch clearing at an oracle price, multi-gate oracle validation with a cross-venue sanity check, and auto-rolling unfilled orders are reusable across on-chain trading venues.

New Idea Opportunities: Inference: the blind batch mechanism generalises to any asset pair with a reliable oracle and would be valuable as a shared settlement layer other Stacks DEXs route large orders into rather than competing with them.

Summary: Xtrata is a low-cost inscription protocol on Stacks for permanent media, data and digital artefacts. It brings Ordinals-style inscriptions to Bitcoin's smart contract layer but treats them as structured, addressable, recursive data blocks designed to be reused and rebuilt on-chain, with SIP-009 compatible assets and a commerce layer on top.
Problem Solved: Ordinals treat inscriptions as isolated artefacts — an image or a piece of metadata that cannot reference or compose with anything else. That makes it impossible to store entire applications, media engines or recursive software modules on Bitcoin, and there is no programmable commerce layer around the resulting assets.
How It Works: A single Xtrata inscription can be as large as a Bitcoin block: data is uploaded in chunks, stored fully on-chain, sealed immutably, and reconstructed deterministically by any client. Because inscriptions are addressable data blocks rather than isolated artefacts, they can be referenced recursively so one inscription composes from others. Assets mint as SIP-009 compatible tokens. On top of storage sits a commerce layer: USDCx-powered entitlement commerce grants paid access without transferring ownership, USDCx and sBTC settle secondary trades, sBTC reserve vaults create premium access states tied to on-chain assets, and x402-style integrations connect on-chain rights to standard web payment flows.

Summary: B2Pix is a non-custodial bridge between sBTC on Stacks and Brazil's PIX instant payment system, letting Brazilians pay electricity bills, buy on Amazon or Mercado Livre, or pay for groceries with Bitcoin — anything that accepts PIX can be paid with sBTC.

Bolt Protocol integration lets users pay transaction fees in sBTC so they never need to hold STX, and an embedded wallet with passkey/WebAuthn authentication removes wallet setup from onboarding. Summary: Shroud Protocol is a zero-knowledge privacy mixer for Casper Network. Users deposit a fixed amount of CSPR into a common pool and receive a cryptographic commitment, then later withdraw the same amount to a different address by proving in zero knowledge that they made a valid deposit without revealing which one.
Problem Solved: Casper has no privacy-preserving infrastructure, so every transaction happens in full public view. That blocks legitimate use cases — protection from front-running, prevention of competitive intelligence gathering, and ordinary financial autonomy — and restricts adoption by privacy-conscious individuals, enterprises needing confidential transactions, and DeFi protocols exposed to MEV extraction.
How It Works: A user deposits a fixed CSPR denomination into a shared pool and receives a commitment proving the deposit without revealing their identity. Withdrawal to a different address requires generating a Groth16 ZK-SNARK proving membership in the deposit set without disclosing which deposit was theirs, which breaks the on-chain link between sender and receiver. MiMC7 is used as the in-circuit hash function for efficiency, and the client uses on-chain-first synchronisation, pulling live state directly from the Casper blockchain rather than trusting an indexer.

Summary: Umbra makes Bitcoin on Starknet genuinely unlinkable rather than merely pseudonymous. A user deposits wBTC anonymously and withdraws to any address with no on-chain link between the two, while the note controlling the deposit is encrypted with a wallet-derived key and pinned to IPFS so only that wallet can recover it.
Problem Solved: Pseudonymous chains leak the entire transaction graph, so wBTC positions on Starknet are fully traceable. Mixers address the on-chain half of the problem but leave a second, less discussed one: the secret note that controls a deposit has to be stored somewhere, and losing it loses the funds while storing it carelessly destroys the privacy.
How It Works: Two layers work together. On-chain, a zero-knowledge Merkle membership proof written in Noir and verified by Garaga breaks the link between depositor and withdrawer, so no address association ever appears on Starknet. Off-chain, the note — a nullifier, secret and commitment triple — is encrypted with AES-GCM under a key derived from the user's wallet signature and the ciphertext is pinned to IPFS via Pinata or Storacha; the plaintext never leaves the browser and the IPFS CID is the only thing the user must remember, since only the depositing wallet can decrypt it. Additional integrations cover Pragma or Chainlink oracles, Vesu for yield on pooled funds, Poseidon2 over BN254 for the Merkle tree, and HTLCs for atomic swaps.

Summary: Kaspa Kinesis is a zero-infrastructure multiplayer engine that uses the Kaspa BlockDAG as both a verifiable randomness source and a global message relay, enabling real-time auditable gameplay with no servers, no matchmaking backend and no NAT-traversal infrastructure.
Problem Solved: Decentralised gaming has two hard blockers. Trusted entropy: a fair game needs randomness neither player can predict or bias, which normally requires a trusted server or an oracle. Peer connectivity: most players sit behind carrier-grade NAT, so direct peer-to-peer connections fail without TURN or STUN relay servers that someone must pay for and operate.
How It Works: Two mechanisms answer those blockers. Recursive Folding is a novel entropy-extraction method that mixes and whitens proof-of-work artefacts from the BlockDAG into NIST-grade randomness — unbiased and verifiable, so fairness-critical applications can rely on it without a trusted party. The Kaspa Relay treats the BlockDAG as a decentralised mailbox, letting two peers both behind carrier-grade NAT exchange messages without TURN or STUN servers, since each writes to and reads from the chain rather than connecting directly. Together they allow a game to run with no managed server of any kind while every action remains auditable on-chain.
Tech Stack: JavaScript and TypeScript; Recursive Folding entropy extraction from proof-of-work artefacts; Kaspa BlockDAG used as a message relay; KKGameEngine with its own developer guide; deployed at kaspakinesis.vercel.app. MIT licensed.
Repository Activity: Public JavaScript repository, MIT licensed, created 2026-01-18 and last pushed 2026-02-27 — eleven days after the hackathon closed — with 3 stars. The repository is organised as a project hub with a separate game-engine guide.

Relay latency and cost per message are also unmeasured, and no third-party game has been built on the engine.

Key Innovation: Using one chain for two unrelated infrastructure roles at once: proof-of-work artefacts are folded and whitened into verifiable entropy, and the same BlockDAG doubles as a decentralised mailbox that lets two carrier-grade-NAT peers communicate without TURN or STUN — removing both the randomness oracle and the relay server from a multiplayer stack.
Core Problem: Building a decentralised multiplayer game requires solving two problems that have nothing to do with the game. Fair randomness needs a source neither player controls, which in practice means trusting a server or an oracle. And most consumer internet connections sit behind carrier-grade NAT, so peers cannot connect directly and need relay infrastructure someone must run and fund. Both reintroduce exactly the centralised operator that decentralised gaming was meant to remove.
Solution: Extract entropy from Kaspa's proof-of-work artefacts through Recursive Folding, producing unbiased verifiable randomness suitable for fairness-critical use, and use the BlockDAG itself as a mailbox relay so two peers behind carrier-grade NAT exchange messages by writing to and reading from the chain. The result is a multiplayer engine with no servers, no matchmaking backend and no NAT-traversal infrastructure, where gameplay remains auditable.
Target Users: Developers building decentralised multiplayer games, and any application needing verifiable randomness or serverless peer messaging.
Unique Insight: A fast public chain is not only a settlement layer — its block production is a continuous stream of both entropy and addressable message slots, which together are most of what a multiplayer backend does.
Differentiation: Differs from VRF oracles by extracting entropy from existing proof-of-work rather than requiring a separate service, and from WebRTC-based peer connectivity by needing no TURN or STUN infrastructure at all.
Reusable Patterns: Entropy extraction and whitening from proof-of-work artefacts, using a chain as a NAT-traversing mailbox relay, and zero-managed-server architectures are reusable well beyond gaming.
Business Model: Inference: not stated. The engine is MIT-licensed infrastructure, so monetisation would have to come from hosted services or from games built on it.
Moat: Inference: not stated. Recursive Folding is the technically distinctive component, but it is published under MIT, so ecosystem adoption rather than exclusivity is the realistic advantage.
Distribution Strategy: Inference: not stated. Shipping a documented game engine alongside a live demo signals a developer-adoption motion.
Key Risks: Relaying game messages through a public chain means every message costs a transaction and inherits block latency, which bounds the genre of games that can work; and the NIST-grade entropy claim is unverified by any published test output.
New Idea Opportunities: Inference: publishing the Recursive Folding test-suite results would convert the entropy claim into a credential other fairness-critical applications could rely on, and the mailbox relay is independently useful for any serverless peer-to-peer application, not only games.

Summary: KasFlow is an open-source payment toolkit for Kaspa built around the first passkey-powered wallet SDK for the network. Users create and use wallets with a fingerprint or Face ID rather than a seed phrase, and payment requests are encoded entirely in URLs so no backend is required.
Problem Solved: Accepting or sending Kaspa payments requires a wallet with a seed phrase and, for merchants, a backend to generate and track payment requests. Both are barriers: seed phrases exclude mainstream users, and a database requirement makes payment links expensive and centralised.
How It Works: The passkey wallet uses WebAuthn/FIDO2 so the device biometric deterministically derives the private key, and the credential syncs across the user's devices through iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager — no seed phrase, no password. Payment requests are encoded directly in URLs using base64url, so there is no database, no server cost, the links work on any static host and the system stays decentralised. Kaspa's sub-second block times make the resulting confirmation visible almost immediately, which the toolkit visualises. The SDK is published on npm as @kasflow/passkey-wallet with separate documentation.

On the merchant side, generating and tracking payment requests normally means running a backend with a database, which costs money, introduces a central point of failure and puts payment infrastructure out of reach for individuals and small sellers.
Solution: Derive the Kaspa wallet key deterministically from a WebAuthn passkey so the user authenticates with a fingerprint or Face ID and the credential syncs through their existing platform keychain, and encode payment requests entirely in base64url URLs so a request is just a link — no database, no server, hostable on any static site — with Kaspa's sub-second confirmations visualised as the payment lands.

Defensively it simulates state diffs inline with LiteSVM to block honeypot transactions before they are sent; offensively it enables sub-millisecond Monte Carlo simulation for quantitative trading, with no SaaS round trip in the path.

The same local execution environment is reused for fast Monte Carlo simulation, which is only viable because there is no remote call in the loop. The founder states the idea came from running a passive node and watching thousands of bots fail transactions.

Problem Solved: Base-layer confirmation latency makes a synchronized 60-second multiplayer game feel slow and fragmented, while server-selected randomness would force players to trust the operator. BlitzMine needs real-time shared state without giving the backend control over the outcome.

Summary: Wraith is a full privacy layer on Stellar. Assets move into a shielded pool where holding, paying and trading all work like a normal wallet except amounts and participants stay hidden, with every action verified on-chain by Soroban contracts and nothing custodied.
Problem Solved: On Stellar every balance, payment and trade is public, so ordinary use exposes a complete financial profile. Privacy attempts elsewhere typically break the wallet experience or require custody; the challenge is providing hiding without changing how a wallet feels or who holds the funds.
How It Works: A deposit converts assets into notes — commitments in an on-chain Merkle tree that reveal nothing about who owns what. To withdraw, send or trade, the wallet builds an UltraHonk proof written in Noir that the Soroban contract verifies on-chain: it proves the user owns a valid note and is not double-spending, without revealing the note, the amount or the counterparty. A valid proof moves funds and no proof moves nothing. On top of the shielded layer sit deposit and withdraw for classic Stellar assets such as XLM and USDC, a hidden multi-asset portfolio only the owner can see, private payments where the recipient shares a receive code rather than a public address, and a dark-pool DEX with hidden orders. The team also built a private Ethereum-to-Stellar bridge into the shielded layer.
Tech Stack: Noir circuits with UltraHonk proving verified on-chain by Soroban contracts; TypeScript, Rust and Solidity components; Merkle-tree note commitments; Docker packaging.

Key Innovation: Making the shielded layer feel like an ordinary wallet rather than a mixer: notes are the internal representation, but the user simply holds a portfolio, pays with a receive code and trades on a dark-pool order book — so privacy is the default state of a normal account rather than a separate deposit-and-withdraw ritual.
Core Problem: Public ledgers make every balance, counterparty and trade permanently visible, which is unacceptable for payroll, business payments and anyone whose position size is itself information. Existing privacy tools solve one transaction type — usually a transfer — and force the user in and out of a special pool for each action, so the moment they want to hold, pay and trade privately they are back to leaking on every step outside the mixer.
Solution: Turn deposits into Merkle-tree note commitments and make every subsequent action — withdraw, send, trade — a Noir UltraHonk proof that a Soroban contract verifies on-chain, proving note ownership and no double-spend without revealing note, amount or counterparty. Around that primitive, ship the whole surface a user needs: multi-asset hidden portfolio, private payments addressed by receive code, and a dark-pool DEX with hidden orders.
Target Users: Stellar users and businesses needing confidential balances, payments and trading rather than a single private transfer.
Unique Insight: Privacy fails at the seams — the moment a user must leave the shielded layer to do anything useful, the exit leaks what the pool concealed, so the pool has to support the whole workflow.
Differentiation: Differs from mixers by supporting holding, paying and trading inside the shielded layer, and from privacy chains by adding the layer to Stellar without requiring migration.
Reusable Patterns: Note-commitment Merkle pools, receive codes instead of public addresses, dark-pool order books over shielded balances, and Noir plus Soroban on-chain verification are reusable across privacy protocols.
Business Model: Inference: not stated. A shielded DEX would conventionally take a swap fee, with deposits and withdrawals free to encourage pool depth.
Moat: Inference: not stated. Anonymity-set size is the product and it compounds, so the first shielded pool on a chain to accumulate depth is very hard to displace.
Distribution Strategy: Inference: not stated. Integration into Stellar wallets would let users shield without discovering a separate application.
Key Risks: An unaudited shielded pool holding user assets across four distinct features is a large attack surface where a single circuit flaw drains everything; and privacy pools face escalating regulatory pressure with no compliance path described.
New Idea Opportunities: Inference: adding optional view keys would let a business use the pool for payroll while still satisfying an auditor, and the note-and-proof primitive could be published as a Soroban library other Stellar apps shield with.

Summary: AnchorShield lets a person prove they are allowed to move money or hold a regulated asset without showing who they are. One real identity check becomes a wallet-bound, policy-tagged attestation that any Stellar app can verify as a reusable KYC passport, with no raw identity touching the ledger.
Problem Solved: Financial rules require checks — identity-verified, not sanctioned, old enough, in an allowed country — and on a normal blockchain the only way to enforce them is to publish identity information: lists of approved wallets, identity badges tied to addresses. Because a blockchain is public and permanent, that makes everyone's compliance status visible to the world forever. Compliance is bought by destroying privacy.
How It Works: A user connects a standard Stellar wallet (Freighter) and completes one live Sumsub identity verification, the same service real financial institutions use. From that single credential the holder can prove KYC status, sanctions and revocation non-membership, age and jurisdiction in zero knowledge. The result is a wallet-bound, policy-tagged attestation that functions as a reusable passport across the ecosystem, so payments and real-world-asset transfers are gated on-chain while the chain verifies only that a proof is genuine and learns nothing about the person behind it.
Tech Stack: Circom circuits with Rust and JavaScript components; Sumsub as the regulated identity issuer; Freighter wallet integration; wallet-bound policy-tagged attestations; revocation non-membership proofs; CI configured with a release branch. Apache-2.0 licensed.

Key Innovation: Proving revocation non-membership alongside KYC, sanctions, age and jurisdiction from a single credential, so the attestation stays valid as a passport without the chain holding a live allowlist — this is the piece that lets one verification be reused across apps instead of expiring into a stale badge.
Core Problem: Regulated activity on a public ledger forces an impossible trade. To enforce that a counterparty is verified, not sanctioned, old enough and in an allowed jurisdiction, someone must publish that status on-chain — and a blockchain is public and permanent, so every user's compliance record becomes a permanent public profile linkable across every application they ever touch. The alternative, per-app verification, multiplies both the data collection and the breach surface.
Solution: Anchor one live Sumsub identity check to the user's Stellar wallet and derive a zero-knowledge attestation from it that proves KYC status, sanctions and revocation non-membership, age and jurisdiction as needed. The attestation is wallet-bound and policy-tagged so any Stellar app can gate payments or regulated-asset transfers on it, while the ledger sees only that a valid proof exists and never the identity behind it.
Target Users: Stellar applications handling regulated assets or payments, anchors, and users who need compliant access without publishing identity.
Unique Insight: Compliance requires a decision rather than a dossier, and once that distinction is made the whole regime can run on proofs — which also removes the per-app data collection that makes compliance expensive.
Differentiation: Differs from on-chain allowlists by publishing nothing, and from single-use KYC by producing a reusable wallet-bound passport that carries revocation state.
Reusable Patterns: Wallet-bound reusable credentials, revocation non-membership proofs, policy-tagged attestations, and anchoring ZK identity to a regulated issuer are reusable across compliance infrastructure.
Business Model: Inference: not stated. Compliance layers conventionally charge per verification or license to the applications that gate on them.
Moat: Inference: not stated. The credential pool compounds with each verified user and cannot be ported, which is the same structural advantage every identity network relies on.

Summary: Diam is a confidential on-chain OTC desk built on iExec Nox. Trade amounts stay encrypted on-chain inside trusted execution environments, and a sealed-bid Vickrey request-for-quote settles the trade without leaking losing bids — institutional size privacy without leaving the chain.

The result is that RWA issuance keeps stalling at pilot stage, because the privacy, compliance and auditability requirements have never been satisfiable at the same time.
Solution: Build the control plane out of ERC-7984 confidential tokens on iExec Nox with browser-generated proofs, and add the three pieces a transparent token lacks: a transfer controller enforcing who may hold and move the asset, a selective disclosure registry so a holder can reveal a specific fact to a specific party, and an audit anchor recording that transfers and disclosures occurred. Wrap it in an operational dashboard covering onboarding, issuance, investor mapping, compliance passports, audit trails and settlement.
Target Users: RWA issuers, compliance officers administering restricted assets, and institutional investors requiring position confidentiality.
Unique Insight: Institutional privacy is not one requirement but three conflicting ones — confidentiality from the public, disclosure to a counterparty, and provability to a regulator — and only a design that separates them can satisfy all three.
Differentiation: Differs from transparent RWA tokens by encrypting balances and amounts natively, and from generic confidential tokens by shipping the transfer control, disclosure and audit layers an issuer actually needs.
Reusable Patterns: Separating confidentiality, selective disclosure and audit anchoring into distinct primitives, browser-generated confidential proofs, and role-based operational dashboards are reusable across regulated asset infrastructure.
Business Model: Inference: not stated. Asset-tokenisation platforms conventionally charge issuers a setup fee plus basis points on assets under administration.
Moat: Inference: not stated. Issuer relationships and regulatory acceptance of the disclosure model are the durable assets; the contracts are replicable.
Distribution Strategy: Inference: not stated. Selling to issuers and their compliance functions rather than to investors is the standard route for this category.
Key Risks: The hardest part of RWA is the off-chain legal claim and none of it is addressed, so the platform solves the second problem before the first; and an unaudited confidential token holding regulated assets is a severe exposure.
New Idea Opportunities: Inference: the selective disclosure registry is independently valuable to any regulated on-chain asset and could be published as a standard, and compliance passports would be more useful shared across issuers than rebuilt per platform.

Summary: DarkOdds is a permissionless prediction market on Arbitrum Sepolia where markets and odds are public but bet sizes are encrypted. Separately, confidential prediction markets need division on encrypted values to compute proportional pari-mutuel payouts, and pure fully homomorphic encryption struggles with division. Payouts are selective-disclosure and TEE-signed, so a winner receives a cryptographic receipt they can show an accountant or keep sealed permanently. Market creation is permissionless with ChainGPT-powered deployment, so anyone can list a market on anything without a curation gate.

Summary: Chickenz is a real-time competitive 2D platformer shooter where the full match input transcript is replayed inside a RISC Zero zkVM to produce a proof of the outcome, which a Soroban contract verifies on-chain — so the chain knows who won without trusting the game server.
Problem Solved: Competitive online games settle outcomes on a server the players must trust. Once prizes are attached, that trust is worth exploiting, and no player can verify that the reported winner is the actual winner. Running the game itself on-chain is impossible at 60Hz.
How It Works: Two players fight best-of-three rounds of 30 seconds each with one life per round, five weapon types spawning on the map and a sudden-death mechanic that closes the arena walls at 20 seconds. At match start the server calls start_game() on the Game Hub contract with both players' wallets and a committed seed hash. During play the server records every input from every tick of a 60Hz deterministic simulation. At match end the two winning rounds' input transcripts are replayed inside a RISC Zero zkVM guest, Groth16 compression produces a 260-byte seal and a 76-byte journal, and a Soroban contract calls a Nethermind Groth16 verifier over BN254 pairings and validates that the seed commitment matches. Off-chain compute, on-chain verification.
Tech Stack: TypeScript and Rust with Bun runtime; 60Hz deterministic simulation; RISC Zero zkVM guest replaying input transcripts; Groth16 compression to a 260-byte seal and 76-byte journal; Nethermind Groth16 BN254 verifier called from a Soroban contract; Boundless verifiable compute. Core Problem: Competitive games with prizes have a settlement problem that gets worse as the stakes rise. Putting the game on-chain is not an option — a 60Hz action game generates thousands of state transitions per match — so on-chain gaming has settled for turn-based designs or trusted operators.
Solution: Keep the game off-chain and prove it afterwards. Commit a seed hash on-chain at match start, run a deterministic 60Hz simulation recording every input, then replay the two winning rounds inside a RISC Zero zkVM and compress the proof with Groth16 into a 260-byte seal and 76-byte journal. A Soroban contract verifies the proof through a Nethermind BN254 verifier and checks the seed commitment, so the chain independently establishes the winner.
Target Users: Competitive players in prize-bearing matches, and developers of real-time games needing trustless outcome settlement.
Unique Insight: Determinism is what makes a fast game provable — if the outcome is a pure function of inputs, the expensive part can happen off-chain and only the proof needs to be on-chain.
Differentiation: Differs from on-chain games by keeping real-time play off-chain entirely, and from server-authoritative esports platforms by making the result cryptographically verifiable rather than reported.
Reusable Patterns: Deterministic simulation with input-transcript replay in a zkVM, seed commitments binding randomness before play, and Groth16 compression for cheap on-chain verification are reusable across verifiable compute.
Business Model: Inference: not stated. Competitive games with verifiable outcomes conventionally take a rake on entry fees or tournament pools.
Moat: Inference: not stated. The proving pipeline is genuinely hard engineering, but player liquidity decides whether a competitive game survives.
Distribution Strategy: Inference: not stated. A live browser-playable game at its own domain is a direct consumer channel.
Key Risks: Proof generation cost per match is unpublished and could exceed the value being settled; and the server remains the sole recorder of inputs, so transcript completeness is a residual trust assumption the seed commitment does not remove.
New Idea Opportunities: Inference: the deterministic-sim-plus-zkVM settlement pipeline is more valuable than the game and could be packaged for other real-time titles, and verified match history would support skill-rated wagering with provable outcomes.

Summary: Stellar Poker is on-chain Texas Hold'em with genuinely private cards, using coSNARKs — zero-knowledge multi-party computation — so no single party ever sees a player's hand. A committee of MPC nodes running TACEO coNoir shuffles and deals using REP3 secret sharing and generates UltraHonk proofs verified on-chain for every deal, reveal and showdown.
Problem Solved: The builder states the underlying constraint precisely: it is impossible to shuffle cards between multiple players using zero-knowledge proofs alone without a centralised intermediary. Every on-chain card game therefore either trusts a dealer with the deck or is not really private, and most projects gloss over this rather than solving it.
How It Works: Instead of a single dealer, a committee of MPC nodes running TACEO coNoir performs the shuffle and deal under REP3 secret sharing, so the deck exists only as shares and no individual node can reconstruct any hand. The committee then produces UltraHonk zero-knowledge proofs that each deal, reveal and showdown was performed correctly, and those proofs are verified on-chain by Soroban contracts. The builder also published a reusable crate so other Soroban applications can do card shuffling, and a slide deck explaining why ZK alone cannot solve multi-party shuffling.

Zero-knowledge proofs can hide a card once it exists, but they cannot generate a shuffle that no participant can predict without someone holding the deck — so projects either accept a centralised dealer, which reintroduces exactly the trust that on-chain play was meant to remove, or quietly ship a game where the operator can see every hand.
